summary: Maduru Oya National Park was created in 1983 over ancestral lands of Dambana Vedda communities; park law restricted entry/residence and communities were resettled in Mahaweli settlements, with only limited later sanctuary concessions.
verification_target: FFPO, cabinet documentation, Mahaweli records and Cambridge synthesis
drift_risk: describing all Vedda communities as displaced in the same way or reducing all later cultural change to one intervention

summary: Where subsistence practices, ritual places, vocabulary and ecological knowledge depend on forest access, legal/physical separation from territory is a plausible mechanism of cultural disruption; it is an amplifier rather than a complete monocausal explanation of assimilation.
verification_target: triangulate land-use restrictions with language, religion and livelihood studies
drift_risk: erasing adaptation, agency and community variation

summary: Research at Yakkure and Henanigala documents substantial Buddhist/Hindu religious borrowing following resettlement while remnants of Na Yakku-associated ritual remain; this supports cultural transformation under pressure rather than a binary intact/disappeared culture.
verification_target: retain study scope to Yakkure/Henanigala and compare with Dambana before generalization
drift_risk: generalizing two community case studies to every Vedda group

summary: Current Vedda population size remains unresolved for corpus purposes because historical estimates and modern identity categories are not directly comparable; the old guide phrase 'a few hundred' must not be promoted as a current metric.
verification_target: recent census methodology, community self-identification and specialist demographic work
drift_risk: false precision in population decline narratives
